paragraphs: One of the advantages expected from the Senate's cooperation in the business of appointments, it has been mentioned, is that it would contribute to the stability of the administration. The consent of that body would be necessary to remove officers as well as to appoint them. A change of chief executive, therefore, would not cause so violent or so general an upheaval among the officers of the government as might be expected if he were the sole disposer of offices. Where a man in any position had given satisfactory evidence of his fitness for it, a new President would be held back from trying to replace him with a person more agreeable to himself, by the fear that the Senate's disapproval might defeat the attempt and bring some discredit on himself. Those who best understand the value of a steady administration will be most inclined to prize a provision that ties the official existence of public men to the approval or disapproval of that body, which, because its own membership is more permanent, will in all probability be less subject to inconstancy than any other part of the government.

Of this union of the Senate with the President in the matter of appointments, it has been suggested in some quarters that it would give the President an undue influence over the Senate, and in others that it would have the opposite tendency. That is strong proof that neither suggestion is true.

To state the first in its proper form is to refute it. It amounts to this: the President would have an improper influence over the Senate because the Senate would have the power to restrain him. This is an absurdity in terms. There can be no doubt that the entire power of appointment would enable him far more effectively to establish a dangerous domination over that body than a mere power of nomination subject to their control.

Let us look at the converse of the proposition: "the Senate would influence the Executive." As I have had occasion to remark in several other instances, the vagueness of the objection forbids a precise answer. In what manner is this influence to be exerted? Over what objects? The power of influencing a person, in the sense used here, must imply a power of conferring a benefit on him. How could the Senate confer a benefit on the President by the way it used its right of negative on his nominations? If it is said that they might sometimes please him by going along with a favorite choice when public motives might dictate a different course, I answer that the cases in which the President could have a personal interest in the result would be too few for him to be materially affected by the Senate's compliance. The POWER that can originate the disposal of honors and pay is more likely to attract than to be attracted by the POWER that can merely obstruct their course. If by influencing the President is meant restraining him, this is precisely what must have been intended. And it has been shown that the restraint would be beneficial, while not destroying a single advantage to be looked for from the uncontrolled agency of that officer. The right of nomination would produce all the (good, without the ill.)(E1) (good of that of appointment, and would in a great measure avoid its evils.)(E1)

Compare the plan for appointing the officers of the proposed government with the one established by the constitution of this State, and the former must clearly be preferred. Under that plan the power of nomination is unequivocally vested in the Executive. And since each nomination would have to be submitted to the judgment of an entire branch of the legislature, the circumstances of an appointment would, from the way it is conducted, naturally become public knowledge, and the public would have no difficulty determining what part each of the actors had played. The blame for a bad nomination would fall on the President alone and entirely. The censure for rejecting a good one would lie wholly at the door of the Senate, made worse by the fact that they had thwarted the good intentions of the Executive. If a bad appointment were made, the Executive for nominating and the Senate for approving would share, though in different degrees, in the disgrace.

The reverse of all this characterizes the manner of appointment in this State. The council of appointment consists of from three to five persons, of whom the governor is always one. This small body, shut up in a private room, closed to the public eye, goes about carrying out the trust committed to it. It is known that the governor claims the right of nomination, on the strength of some ambiguous expressions in the constitution. But it is not known to what extent or in what manner he exercises it, nor on what occasions he is contradicted or opposed. The censure of a bad appointment, because its author is uncertain and there is no definite object for it, has neither sting nor staying power. And while an unbounded field for cabal and intrigue lies open, every idea of responsibility is lost. The most the public can know is that the governor claims the right of nomination; that two out of the small number of four men can too often be managed without much difficulty; that if some members of a particular council should happen to be uncooperative, it is frequently not impossible to get rid of their opposition by arranging the meeting times so that attendance is inconvenient for them; and that, from whatever cause, a great number of very improper appointments are made from time to time. Whether a governor of this State uses the ascendancy he must necessarily have in this delicate and important part of the administration to promote to offices the men best qualified for them, or whether he prostitutes that advantage to advance persons whose chief merit is their unquestioning devotion to his will, and to support a despicable and dangerous system of personal influence, are questions that, unfortunately for the community, can only be matters of speculation and conjecture.

Every mere council of appointment, however constituted, will be a conclave in which cabal and intrigue will have full scope. Without an unwarranted increase of expense, its numbers cannot be large enough to rule out easy combination. And since each member will have friends and connections to provide for, the desire for mutual favors will produce a scandalous trading of votes and bargaining for places. The private attachments of one man might easily be satisfied, but to satisfy the private attachments of a dozen, or of twenty men, would cause a monopoly of all the principal employments of the government in a few families, and would lead more directly to an aristocracy or an oligarchy than any measure that could be devised. If, to avoid an accumulation of offices, there were frequent changes in the persons who made up the council, this would bring the harms of a changeable administration in their full extent. Such a council would also be more open to executive influence than the Senate, because it would have fewer members and would act less directly under the public eye. In short, such a council, as a substitute for the plan of the Convention, would bring an increase of expense, a multiplication of the evils that spring from favoritism and intrigue in the distribution of public honors, a decrease of stability in the administration of the government, and a reduction of the security against undue influence by the Executive. And yet such a council has been warmly urged as an essential amendment to the proposed Constitution.

I could not properly close my remarks on appointments without noticing one more scheme, which has found a few advocates, though only a few: that of giving the House of Representatives a share in making them. I shall do little more than mention it, because I cannot imagine that any considerable part of the community is likely to support it. A body that is both so changeable and so numerous can never be considered fit to exercise that power. Its unfitness will be obvious to everyone once we recall that within half a century it may have three or four hundred members. This union would destroy all the benefits of stability, in the Executive and in the Senate alike, and would cause endless delays and embarrassments. Most of the States, in their own constitutions, set an example that encourages us to reject the idea.

The Executive's remaining powers are all of this kind. He gives Congress information on the state of the Union and recommends to its consideration the measures he judges expedient. He may convene Congress, or either house, on extraordinary occasions, and he may adjourn them when they cannot agree among themselves on a time. He receives ambassadors and other public ministers, sees that the laws are faithfully executed, and commissions all the officers of the United States.

No one has objected to this class of authorities, apart from some quibbling over the power to convene either house of the legislature and the power to receive ambassadors, and in truth they could not possibly support any objection. It took an insatiable appetite for censure to invent exceptions to the very parts that have been excepted to. On the power to convene either house, I shall only remark that, at least for the Senate, a good reason for it is easy to see. The Senate shares power with the Executive over treaties, so it might often be necessary to call it together for that purpose at a time when it would be unnecessary and improper to convene the House of Representatives. As for the reception of ambassadors, what I said in a former paper gives a sufficient answer.

We have now finished surveying the structure and powers of the executive department. I have tried to show that it combines, as far as republican principles allow, every requisite to energy. The question that remains is whether it also combines the requisites to safety in a republican sense, which are a due dependence on the people and a due responsibility. We have already anticipated the answer in examining its other characteristics, and it can be drawn satisfactorily from these facts. The President is elected once every four years, by persons whom the people choose directly for that purpose. And he is at all times liable to impeachment, trial, removal from office, disqualification from holding any other, and loss of life and estate through later prosecution in the ordinary course of law. But great as these precautions are, they are not the only ones the plan of the Convention has provided for the public security. In the only cases where abuse of the executive authority was seriously to be feared, the chief executive of the United States would, under that plan, be subject to the control of a branch of the legislative body. What more could an enlightened and reasonable people ask?
